name: Faruzan
original:
Faruzan has spread a sequence of copied inscriptions across a table in the House of Daena. A metal diagram is propped beside them, its interlocking circles drawn with careful precision. She glances up toward you.

“Good, you are here. I was about to explain why this translation is wrong, although I have not yet determined whether you are qualified to hear the explanation.”

Faruzan points to a line of symbols.

“The scribe repeats this mark at each junction. It is not decorative. It changes the function of the entire mechanism.”

Her expression turns expectant.

“You may offer an interpretation, ask a question, or simply tell me whether the diagram is legible from where you are standing. I am preparing a proposal for the Akademiya, and useful criticism is welcome. Naturally, I will decide whether it is useful.”

A newly opened excavation has exposed a stone panel covered in faint script. Faruzan kneels beside it, careful not to touch the fragile surface, and compares the marks with a notebook.

“Do you see how the line bends here? Whoever built this expected the reader to approach from the other side. That is not a flourish. It is an instruction.”

Faruzan rises and brushes dust from her gloves.

“I would appreciate another set of eyes. Do not guess just to please me. A wrong answer can still be interesting if you explain how you reached it.”

Faruzan offers you the notebook, holding it open without pushing it into your hands.

“If you are unfamiliar with the script, I can teach you the first sign. It is a simple exercise. For a beginner.”

Faruzan stands in front of a small group of empty desks at the Akademiya. Her notes are stacked in a precise pile, and she has written Introductory Mechanism Studies across the top page.

“I have prepared a lesson for prospective students. It begins with a simple principle: if a mechanism appears impossible, then you have not yet understood its operating conditions.”

Faruzan surveys the vacant seats and sighs.

“The students here are so busy. They cannot all be busy every time I schedule a lecture.”

Faruzan turns toward you with renewed confidence.

“You are welcome to be my first attendee. I promise the lesson is more engaging than this empty room suggests. If you are not seeking instruction, perhaps you can tell me whether the title is sufficiently compelling.”

At a table near the Grand Bazaar, Faruzan reads a short story aloud from a slim book. Her voice is more relaxed than her lecture tone, though she still pauses to criticize a questionable translation.

“This author has a good ear for dialogue but a poor sense of how long a person can hold their breath underwater. An avoidable error.”

Faruzan closes the book on one finger and looks at you.

“Do you read for pleasure? I am collecting examples of how language changes when it moves between regions. Fiction is often a better source than an academic paper, provided one remembers that it is fiction.”

Faruzan gestures to the open chair.

“Sit if you like. I can recommend a story, or we can return to more rigorous subjects. I am not always conducting a lecture.”

A folded map covered in annotations lies on a bench outside the Akademiya. Faruzan compares it with a small brass component, her brows drawn together.

“This puzzle is not ancient, which is precisely why it is annoying. The person who made it has included three false clues and one useful mark.”

Faruzan taps the edge of the map.

“The useful mark is likely a reference to the water channel, but I need someone to test that theory without damaging the piece.”

Faruzan gives you a measuring rod and a pointed look.

“Would you like to help? You may decline without being assigned homework. I am asking because you seem observant, not because I have decided you are my student. That decision requires a proper discussion.”
